lessons.title: AI Office, AI Board, and Germany's authority structure
lessons.subtitle: Who supervises a mid-sized company: the EU level, the BNetzA and sectoral authorities

sections.title: EU level: AI Office and European AI Board
sections.content:
The **AI Office** (European Artificial Intelligence Office) sits in the Commission's Directorate-General CNECT, with more than 125 staff in six units, including Regulation and Compliance and AI Safety. Article 88 gives it **exclusive supervisory powers over GPAI models** such as GPT-4, Claude and Gemini.

It coordinates the codes of practice, runs the secretariat of the European AI Board and has operated the public Service Desk since 8 October 2025.

The **European AI Board** (Article 65) has one representative per Member State, coordinates the national authorities and advises the Commission. A company that deploys AI and places no GPAI model on the market normally deals with neither directly; its competent authorities sit in Germany.

sections.title: Germany: the Federal Network Agency as the fallback authority
sections.content:
Article 70(2) requires every Member State to name a **single point of contact**. In Germany the AI Market Implementation Act (KI-MIG) names the **Federal Network Agency (Bundesnetzagentur, BNetzA)**. The Bundestag adopted it on **11 June 2026**, the Bundesrat passed it on **10 July 2026** without referral to the Mediation Committee, and it **entered into force on 29 July 2026**.

The BNetzA is now the market-surveillance authority for every area without sectoral supervision, and the single point of contact and complaints body. The Act provides for a **Coordination and Competence Centre (KoKIVO)** inside the agency and an independent market-surveillance chamber for specified areas. The reporting channel in an individual case follows the sector and its law.

sections.title: Sectoral supervision: which other authorities retain jurisdiction
sections.content:
The BNetzA is the fallback authority. Article 74 assigns market surveillance in several areas to existing sectoral authorities; data-protection and other sector-specific law keep their own allocations.

- **Financial institutions:** Article 74(6) generally refers to the authorities responsible under financial-services law.
- **Products covered by Annex I:** market surveillance generally follows the relevant product-safety law (Article 74(3)).
- **Annex III, point 1 (where used for law enforcement, border management, justice or democracy) and points 6 to 8:** under Article 74(8), data-protection supervisory authorities or another authority so designated supervise.

For every system, record purpose, role, sector and the authorities that may have jurisdiction. Have this mapping confirmed legally.

quiz.questionText: Which authority does the KI-MIG name as the single point of contact under Article 70(2)?

answerOptions.text: The Federal Commissioner for Data Protection (BfDI)
The Federal Network Agency (BNetzA)
The Federal Office for Information Security (BSI)
The Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs (BMWK)

quiz.explanation: The KI-MIG, in force since 29 July 2026, names the Federal Network Agency. The competent authority in an individual case still follows the sector and its law.

quiz.questionText: A bank uses an AI system for credit scoring. Which German authority is the market-surveillance authority under Article 74(6)?

answerOptions.text: BNetzA
BaFin
BfDI
DAkkS

quiz.explanation: Article 74(6) gives market surveillance of AI at financial institutions to the financial supervisor, in Germany BaFin. The same model in the bank's HR department falls to the BNetzA.

quiz.questionText: What is the AI Office's primary function?

answerOptions.text: Direct supervision of every AI application used by an SME
The authority responsible for fines under Article 99
Exclusive supervision of GPAI models and coordination at EU level (Article 88)
Certification of AI regulatory sandboxes in the Member States

quiz.explanation: The AI Office (DG CNECT) has exclusive powers over GPAI models under Article 88. AI use in SMEs belongs to national authorities under Article 70, in Germany mainly the BNetzA.

lessons.title: Fines of up to EUR 35 million or 7 percent
lessons.subtitle: The three penalty tiers under Article 99, and what they mean at EUR 20 million turnover

sections.title: The three penalty tiers under Article 99
sections.content:
Article 99 of the AI Act sets three tiers of fines.

**Tier 1: prohibited AI practices (Article 5).** Up to **EUR 35,000,000 or 7 percent of total worldwide annual turnover**, whichever is higher (Article 99(3)). Examples: social scoring, emotion recognition in the workplace, real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces.

**Tier 2: most operator obligations.** Up to **EUR 15,000,000 or 3 percent**, whichever is higher (Article 99(4)). That covers provider obligations (Article 16), authorised representatives (Article 22), importers (Article 23), distributors (Article 24), **deployer obligations (Article 26)** and **transparency obligations (Article 50)**.

**Tier 3: incorrect information to authorities.** Up to **EUR 7,500,000 or 1 percent**, whichever is higher (Article 99(5)), for incorrect, incomplete or misleading information, for example to the BNetzA.

sections.title: The SME rule: the lower amount applies
sections.content:
Large companies face the **higher** of the two amounts, fixed figure or percentage; under Article 99(6), SMEs including start-ups face the **lower** one. At EUR 20 million annual turnover, that caps a fine for a prohibited practice at EUR 1.4 million (7 percent) instead of EUR 35 million.

Article 99(7) requires the authority to weigh **10 factors**, such as severity, number of people affected, intent or negligence, company size, cooperation and **technical and organisational measures** (point (g)). Records of Article 4 training, a risk register and an incident process count there but guarantee no particular reduction.

sections.title: Worked examples for SMEs
sections.content:
**Example A: machinery manufacturer, EUR 20 million turnover**

- Tier 1, say emotion recognition at the factory gate: at most EUR 1.4 million (7 percent).
- Tier 2, say a missing risk assessment for HR AI: at most EUR 600,000 (3 percent).
- Tier 3, incorrect information to the BNetzA: at most EUR 200,000 (1 percent).

**Example B: craft business, EUR 1.5 million turnover**

- Tier 1: at most EUR 105,000 (7 percent), existential for a three-person business.

**Example C: SME with EUR 50 million turnover**

- Tier 2: at most EUR 1.5 million (3 percent, Article 99(4)).

The actual amount depends on proportionality and the documented measures. In Germany the competent market-surveillance authority imposes sanctions under the Act on Regulatory Offences (OWiG); the fine notice can be challenged by objection, on which the local court (Amtsgericht) decides (Article 99(10)). Member States report to the Commission annually (Article 99(11)).

quiz.questionText: What is the maximum fine for a prohibited AI practice under Article 5?

answerOptions.text: Up to EUR 7.5 million or 1 percent
Up to EUR 15 million or 3 percent
Up to EUR 35 million or 7 percent, whichever is higher
Up to EUR 50 million or 10 percent

quiz.explanation: Article 99(3): up to EUR 35 million or 7 percent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. For SMEs, Article 99(6) applies the lower amount.

quiz.questionText: Which fine rule does Article 99(6) apply to SMEs, including start-ups?

answerOptions.text: A fixed 50-percent reduction in the fine
The lower of the fixed amount and the percentage amount applies
Complete exemption from fines for the first three years
Fines are capped at EUR 10,000 regardless of the infringement

quiz.explanation: For SMEs the lower of the fixed amount and the percentage applies. At EUR 20 million turnover, the Tier 1 ceiling is EUR 1.4 million instead of EUR 35 million.

quiz.questionText: Which fine tier covers incorrect or misleading information given to a market-surveillance authority?

answerOptions.text: Tier 1: up to EUR 35 million or 7 percent
Tier 2: up to EUR 15 million or 3 percent
Tier 3: up to EUR 7.5 million or 1 percent
No fine tier applies; only a warning may be issued

quiz.explanation: Article 99(5) covers incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or authorities. That is Tier 3.

lessons.title: AI regulatory sandboxes: free testing arrangements for SMEs
lessons.subtitle: What Article 57 provides, what the AI Omnibus changed and what operates in Germany

sections.title: What an AI regulatory sandbox is under Article 57
sections.content:
If you build a high-risk AI system, you can talk to the authority before placing it on the market: in an **AI regulatory sandbox**. Under Article 3, point (55), that is a controlled framework in which a competent authority lets a provider or prospective provider develop, train, validate and, where appropriate, test an innovative AI system in real-world conditions.

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (the AI Omnibus), applicable since 27 July 2026, sets **2 August 2027** in Article 57(1) as the deadline for at least one national sandbox. Article 57 provides, among other things, for guidance, supervision and a written exit report.

sections.title: What SMEs receive under the Regulation
sections.content:
Under Article 58(2), point (d), **SMEs including start-ups get priority, free access**; an authority may recover only exceptional costs, fairly and proportionately.

- **No administrative fines** for infringements of the Regulation where the sandbox plan is followed in good faith (Article 57(12)). Liability to third parties under other law remains.
- **A decision within three months** on the application (Article 58(2), point (a)).
- **Positive account** of the written exit report in a later conformity assessment (Article 57(7)).

An organisation building a high-risk system, for recruitment or as a safety component in machinery, can settle questions **before** market placement. This is an implementation option, not a substitute for the applicable legal duties.

sections.title: Status in Germany: BNetzA, BfDI, and Hesse
sections.content:
The German pilot project in 2025/2026 was run jointly by the **Federal Network Agency**, the **BfDI** and the **Hessian Ministry for Digitalisation**, with two simulated start-up cases on the AI Act and the Medical Device Regulation (MDR). The pilot does not establish an open application process.

The KI-MIG gives the BNetzA tasks in innovation support. Whether it already accepts applications is on its current website: check there first, then write the application.

quiz.questionText: What deadline for at least one national AI regulatory sandbox did Parliament and the Council adopt through the AI Omnibus?

answerOptions.text: By 2 February 2025
By 2 August 2025
By 2 August 2026 under the unchanged original text
By 2 August 2027 under the adopted AI Omnibus

quiz.explanation: Article 57(1) originally named 2 August 2026. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, applicable since 27 July 2026, moves the deadline to 2 August 2027.

quiz.questionText: Who gets priority access to an AI regulatory sandbox under Article 58(2), point (d), and what does it cost?

answerOptions.text: Large companies receive priority; access starts at EUR 50,000
SMEs, including start-ups, receive priority; access is free of charge
Only public authorities receive priority; access is free of charge
All companies have equal access; fees are scaled by turnover

quiz.explanation: Article 58(2), point (d), gives SMEs including start-ups priority and free access. Only exceptional costs may be recovered, fairly and proportionately.

quiz.questionText: Which three authorities jointly ran Germany's AI regulatory-sandbox pilot project in 2025/2026?

answerOptions.text: BSI, BKA, and the Federal Chancellery
BaFin, BfArM, and the Federal Cartel Office
The Federal Network Agency, BfDI, and the Hessian Ministry for Digitalisation
DAkkS, TÜV, and the Fraunhofer Society

quiz.explanation: The three bodies ran the pilot together, with start-up cases under the AI Act and the MDR.

lessons.title: Complaints, incident reports, and requests from the competent authority
lessons.subtitle: Incident reporting under Article 73, complaints under Article 85 and a response plan for authority requests
keyConcepts: right to lodge a complaint under Article 85
right to an explanation under Article 86

sections.title: What providers must report: Articles 72 and 73
sections.content:
Post-market monitoring and serious-incident reporting reach providers once the high-risk rules apply. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 sets 2 December 2027 for standalone Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for high-risk systems embedded in products covered by Annex I.

**Article 72:** the post-market monitoring system collects performance data actively and systematically across the system's lifetime. Its plan belongs in the technical documentation.

**Article 73:** serious incidents go to the competent market-surveillance authority, generally within 15 days, within 10 days for certain incidents resulting in death, and within two days for a widespread infringement or disruption of critical infrastructure. Product-safety and data-protection law may trigger their own channels and periods, which already apply.

sections.title: Who may report you: the right to lodge a complaint under Article 85
sections.content:
**Article 85:** any natural or legal person with grounds to consider that there has been an infringement may lodge a complaint with the relevant market-surveillance authority.

In Germany the **BNetzA is the complaints body** where no sectoral authority has jurisdiction; confirm jurisdiction and the active channel against sectoral law and current information from the authorities.

**Article 86**, subject to its conditions, gives a right to a clear and meaningful explanation of the role a high-risk system listed in Annex III played in the decision-making procedure. It gives no general right to an explanation of every AI output.

sections.title: Authority request: a five-step response plan
sections.content:
Under Article 74 the authority obtains full access to documentation and to training, validation and testing data, including through APIs (Article 74(12)). It gets **source code** only on a reasoned request, once other testing or audit procedures have been exhausted or proved insufficient (Article 74(13)).

If it finds non-compliance, it requires corrective action within **no more than 15 working days** (Article 79(2)). For non-compliance with the prohibition in Article 5, the Union safeguard procedure shortens the objection period to 30 days (Article 81).

**Initial response plan (an implementation control, not a statutory five-step format):**

1. **Acknowledge in writing**, record the deadline, involve legal counsel. Do not hand over source code or training data on reflex.
2. **Open an incident log:** date, request, people involved, information communicated.
3. **Confirm jurisdiction:** the BNetzA, or a sectoral authority such as BaFin, BfArM or an LMA?
4. **Assemble records:** Article 4 measures, risk assessment, post-market monitoring records, declaration of conformity. They may evidence measures under Article 99(7), point (g), but guarantee no lower fine.
5. **Cooperate without giving incorrect information:** incorrect or incomplete information falls within Tier 3, up to EUR 7.5 million or 1 percent (Article 99(5)).

quiz.questionText: Within what period must a provider of a high-risk AI system report a serious incident resulting in death?

answerOptions.text: Two days after becoming aware
10 days after becoming aware
15 days after becoming aware
72 hours after becoming aware

quiz.explanation: After a death, Article 73(4) requires a report immediately once the causal link is established or suspected, within 10 days of awareness at the latest. Otherwise 15 days apply (paragraph 2), two days for a widespread infringement (paragraph 3).

quiz.questionText: Who may lodge a complaint with a market-surveillance authority under Article 85 of the AI Act?

answerOptions.text: Only directly affected natural persons represented by a lawyer
Only recognised consumer organisations and trade unions
Any natural or legal person with grounds to suspect an infringement
Only Member States acting through the single point of contact

quiz.explanation: Article 85 lets any natural or legal person with grounds to suspect an infringement complain, without a lawyer. Article 87 and Directive (EU) 2019/1937 also protect whistleblowers.

quiz.questionText: When may a market-surveillance authority request the source code of a high-risk AI system under Article 74(13)?

answerOptions.text: At any time and without stating reasons
Only after a criminal complaint has been filed against the provider
Only on a reasoned request, when other testing is exhausted or insufficient
Only under a court order

quiz.explanation: Article 74(13) sets two cumulative conditions: access is necessary to assess conformity, and testing or audits based on the provider's data and documentation are exhausted or insufficient.
